_meta.scope: Critical interpretation of Pearl Jam songs played on the Pacaembu 2005-12-02 setlist. Author commentary, not lyrics or translations. Quotations from interviews are short and attributed (fair use). Updated incrementally; see show drawer in the site for the rendered version.

black:
Stone Gossard wrote the music for 'Black' in 1990, when the band was still operating under the Mookie Blaylock name and the song existed as an unfinished demo titled 'E Ballad #1.' It became one of the very first lyrics Eddie Vedder put down when he joined the group, and the result is a portrait of a relationship's end told as a slow, processional mantra rather than a confrontation. The narrator does not blame, plead, or rage; he describes loss the way you might describe weather, while acknowledging that the person leaving still occupies every angle of his attention.

The song's central image, a sun rising in someone else's sky, is the cleanest example of Vedder's early instinct for cosmic-scale heartbreak. Where most breakup songs reduce the world, 'Black' expands it: the lover does not vanish, she becomes celestial, observable, permanent. That single rhetorical move is why the song became a touchstone for an entire generation of listeners who heard their own losses dignified by it.

The band has refused for decades to release 'Black' as a single, and the refusal is itself a piece of the song's mythology. Eddie told Cameron Crowe (PJ20, 2011): 'Some songs are too personal. The minute you let them out of the gate they belong to the radio, and that's not what this one is for.' The decision to keep it as an album cut is the rare case of a major label band protecting a song from its own commercial gravity.

Live, 'Black' is a ritual. Vedder almost never sings the closing line as recorded; instead he extends it into wordless improvisation that frequently breaks his own composure. At Pacaembu in December 2005, late in a set already heavy with rarities, the song landed in its usual position: not a peak, not an encore, but a hollowed-out clearing in the middle of the show where the band stops moving and the audience takes over.
even flow:
'Even Flow' began as a Stone Gossard riff that Mike McCready helped shape into a full arrangement during the Ten sessions in 1991. Gossard told Kim Neely for Five Against One that the band recorded the song over and over before they were satisfied; by various accounts, between fifty and a hundred takes. The released version on Ten was the one Eddie liked least; he preferred the looser, faster take that ended up as a B-side and on Lost Dogs. The recorded tension between perfection and looseness is partly why the song never sits still in concert.

Eddie's lyric is a third-person sketch of a homeless man on the streets of Seattle, a 'he' moving through cold mornings, hand outstretched, watching faces that no longer register as individuals. The song never names a city, a cause, or a politician, but it documents what the early-90s Seattle underclass looked like at street level. Vedder, who had been living rough himself when he flew up from San Diego to audition for the band, was writing what he had recently watched.

What keeps 'Even Flow' from being a protest song in the conventional sense is the title phrase itself, which figures the man's thoughts as fragile creatures he can sense arriving but refuses to let settle on him. That image, fragility met with rejection, is more devastating than any indictment. The narrator is not unable to think; he is unwilling to be still long enough for thought to land. That is the diagnosis the song is making.

In live performance, 'Even Flow' is the canonical McCready showcase: the guitar solo expands, contracts, quotes other songs, and frequently runs past the four-minute mark. By 2005, it had become a kind of pressure-release valve in PJ sets, often placed early to let the band burn off energy before settling into more deliberate material. The Pacaembu version sat seventh in the running order, exactly where it belonged: hot enough to push the show forward, structured enough that the rest of the set could hold its shape.
alive:
'Alive' is the first song in what Eddie Vedder later named the 'Mamasan' trilogy, a three-part autobiographical narrative completed by 'Once' and 'Footsteps.' He wrote it almost immediately after receiving Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament's instrumental demos in San Diego in 1990, and the lyric draws from a moment in his teenage years when his mother told him that the man he had grown up calling 'father' was not his biological parent, and that his real father had recently died. The songs in the trilogy follow that revelation forward through grief, denial, and an act of violence; 'Alive' is the moment of impact.

The song's chorus was, by Eddie's own account, originally a curse. To still be alive, after learning what he had learned, felt to the young Vedder like an undeserved survival, a question rather than a celebration. He explained this transformation directly in PJ20: the audience refused to hear the line as a curse. Night after night, crowds sang it back to him as an affirmation, and over time the meaning of the song shifted under his feet. The curse became a benediction without his permission.

That shift is one of the foundational Pearl Jam stories: a song's meaning being rewritten in real time by the people who love it. Vedder has used that arc as a lens for understanding what the band's relationship to its audience even is. The band offers the material, the crowd decides what it does. By the mid-90s, 'Alive' could no longer be sung quietly; it had become a communal object that the band was caretaking rather than owning.

Live, 'Alive' usually closes the main set or sits near the climax of the second encore. McCready's solo at the end, modeled on a Hendrix lick that Mike has openly cited, is one of the few moments in PJ shows where the band steps back and lets a single instrument carry the room. At Pacaembu 2005, 'Alive' sat 18th in the order, arriving after 'Better Man' as the gravitational center of the late-set climb. The performance is documented on the official bootleg and is one of the more confident readings from the South American Tour.
jeremy:
Eddie Vedder wrote 'Jeremy' after reading a brief news item in the Dallas Morning News about Jeremy Wade Delle, a 15-year-old student at Richardson High School in Texas who shot himself in front of his English class on January 8, 1991. Vedder kept the clipping. He folded into the lyric a second, older memory: a classmate from his own school days in San Diego who had brought a gun to class. The song fuses those two stories into a single composite figure: the unseen, mocked, eventually catastrophic boy whose interior life nobody wanted to read.

The music is Jeff Ament's first co-writing credit on a Pearl Jam song; he constructed the bassline that drives the verse and shaped the architecture that lets the song build from murmur to wail. That structural patience, the way 'Jeremy' takes nearly two minutes before the first chorus arrives, is unusual for a debut-album single. The band trusted the listener to wait, and the waiting is what makes the eventual eruption land.

The song became inseparable from Mark Pellington's 1992 music video, which depicted the act in symbolic flashes intense enough to provoke MTV editing demands and a long-running misinterpretation by viewers who believed Jeremy had shot his classmates rather than himself. The band has spoken about the discomfort of that misreading for decades. Vedder eventually stopped performing the song with any regularity in the 2000s and 2010s after every American school shooting reopened the wound; in interviews around the Avocado tour, he made clear that he found playing 'Jeremy' increasingly unbearable in light of how the country had failed the children the song was about.

At Pacaembu 2005 the song appeared late in the set, 26th of 27. That position matters. By that point the audience already knew the night's emotional arc and was prepared to receive 'Jeremy' as the heavy, deliberate object it has always been rather than as a hit single. The 2005 performance is, by Brazilian fan consensus, one of the more measured readings of the period: less anger, more weight.
yellow ledbetter:
'Yellow Ledbetter' was recorded during the Ten sessions in 1991, then left off the album. It surfaced in 1992 as the B-side to the 'Jeremy' single and lived for years in semi-official limbo before being collected on Lost Dogs in 2003. It has never appeared on a proper Pearl Jam studio album, which is part of the song's strange standing in the catalog: it is one of the most-played live songs in the band's history while remaining, technically, an outtake.

Mike McCready's guitar work is the song's defining element. The main figure is built directly out of the Hendrix vocabulary; 'Little Wing' is the most cited reference, but McCready has spoken in interviews about pulling from 'Bold as Love' and 'May This Be Love' as well. The closing solo is one of the most identifiable in 90s rock guitar; for many fans it is the sonic shorthand for 'a Pearl Jam show is now ending,' since 'Yellow Ledbetter' has closed encores with extraordinary consistency since 1995.

The lyric is famously, almost militantly, unintelligible. Vedder has acknowledged in multiple interviews, including a 2018 Howard Stern appearance, that he wrote much of it as improvised vowel-shapes and never bothered to fix the words. Fans have transcribed dozens of mutually contradictory versions; the band has never released an official lyric sheet. What survives across performances is the shape of a melancholy: a porch, a letter, a beach, a goodbye. The specific words slide.

The title's origin is disputed and the band keeps it that way. Mike has mentioned a friend named Tim Ledbetter, a Vietnam-veteran bandmate from McCready's earlier projects, but no confirmed story attaches 'Yellow' to the name. At Pacaembu 2005 the song occupies its standard slot: the final song of the night, played after 'Jeremy,' with the McCready solo extended past five minutes. It is the only song in the set that the audience could be confident would arrive: the closing rite of every PJ show, observed once again in São Paulo.
go:
'Go' is the opening track of Vs. (1993) and one of the most propulsive songs Pearl Jam ever recorded. Jeff Ament wrote the music, which marked an important turn for the band: Vs. would be the album where the rhythm section asserted equal weight with the guitar players, and 'Go' announced that shift in its first ten seconds. The track was tracked at The Site in Marin County, California in early 1993, in sessions famously fraught with arguments about how much pressure the band was willing to absorb after Ten had moved more than ten million copies.

Vedder's lyric is, in his own description, addressed to a firearm. In a 1993 MTV News spot Vedder explained that the song's pleading second-person voice is directed at a gun. The chorus is a refusal, a request that the object turn away from violence. This is part of a longer Vedder preoccupation with American gun culture that surfaces on 'Glorified G' on the same album and resurfaces ten years later on 'Bu$hleaguer' and 'Down.' Vs. is, more than any other Pearl Jam record, an album of refusals, and 'Go' is its first and most physical refusal.

The arrangement is a model of restraint disguised as aggression. Dave Abbruzzese's drums hit on every beat for the first half of the song before the bridge releases the tension; Stone Gossard's guitar is buried under McCready's lead, which is unusual in the PJ catalog and gives the track a top-heavy feel that suits the panic of the lyric. The choice to put 'Go' first on Vs. was deliberate: in PJ20, Stone discusses how the band wanted listeners to feel ambushed by the new record, and 'Go' was meant to be that ambush.

Live, 'Go' has been a primary set-opener and a re-igniter mid-show. It is rarely buried deep in setlists; the song works as a starting gun. It was particularly favored as an opener during the Riot Act and Pearl Jam (2006) tours and reappeared throughout the Lightning Bolt cycle. The audience response is consistent: from the first downstroke the venue tends to compress visibly toward the stage.

At Pacaembu on December 2, 2005, 'Go' opened the show. The South American Tour 2005 was Pearl Jam's first proper visit to the continent in eleven years, and Vedder treated the opening like a confirmation that the band had finally come back. The bootleg recording captures Eddie's voice cracking slightly in the second verse, which is consistent with the energy he tends to put into first songs of a tour or first songs of a country.
hail hail:
'Hail, Hail' is the third track on No Code (1996), the album where Pearl Jam stopped trying to be the biggest band in the world and started trying to be a band that could survive being a band. The music is Stone Gossard's, with arrangement contributions from McCready, and the lyric is one of the most direct things Vedder has ever written about romantic partnership: a plea to be allowed to belong to someone, made by a narrator who is fully aware that he is hard to love.

The song's central rhetorical move is the inversion of conventional gender vocabulary in the chorus, where the narrator asks his partner whether she is 'woman enough to be my man.' This is not a joke. Vedder has described the line in a few interviews (most thoroughly during a 1996 MTV interview promoting No Code) as a way of saying that the kind of strength he needs from a partner is not feminized softness but a kind of hard companionship that masculine and feminine codes both fail to capture. The line is the philosophical heart of the song.

No Code was a commercial disappointment after Vitalogy (which had moved several million units) and was widely treated by the music press as the album where Pearl Jam threw its audience away. Kim Neely's Five Against One devotes most of a chapter to the band's relief at this. 'Hail, Hail' is the only track on the album that sounds like it could have been a Vitalogy outtake, and that is part of why it was released as the second single: it was a bridge for listeners between the rock band they thought they knew and the more diffuse, experimental record No Code actually was.

The arrangement is a Stone Gossard signature. The verse is built on a riff that hangs on a single chord for longer than most rock songs would allow, and the chorus releases the tension through major-minor ambiguity rather than through a traditional lift. Mike McCready's solo is short and economical, more in the Neil Young vein than the Hendrix one, and ends without resolving, which suits the lyric's open question.

Live, 'Hail, Hail' became a staple of the second half of the No Code touring cycle and has stayed in regular rotation ever since. It is not an opener and not a closer; it is a middle-of-set song that consolidates a set's emotional weight. At Pacaembu 2005 it sat second in the running order, immediately after 'Go,' which is one of the most aggressive openings the band has ever assembled. The choice to follow 'Go' with 'Hail, Hail' is a tonal fingerprint of the South American Tour 2005: the band was leaning into the catalog's hard-rock spine and sequencing the first ten songs of each show as something close to a manifesto.
animal:
'Animal' is the second track on Vs. (1993). The music is Stone Gossard's; the lyric is Vedder's response to the year that followed Ten's success. Vs. was an album made under siege: the band was averaging ten major-label interview requests per week, MTV would not stop playing the 'Jeremy' video, and the band was beginning to discover that fame, in the early-90s American sense, was a thing done to you rather than a thing you accepted. 'Animal' is the diagnostic.

The lyric's most famous line is the opening declaration that there are 'five against one' (a line that Kim Neely later took for the title of her authorized 1998 band biography, Five Against One: The Pearl Jam Story). The five-on-one mathematics is deliberately ambiguous in the song. It can be read as the band against the music industry, the band against the press, or any besieged collective against a single antagonist. Vedder told MTV in 1993 that the line was about the way the band felt during the Vs. recording sessions, when nobody outside the five members of the group seemed to be working toward the same goals.

The song's central image, and the source of its title, is the comparative preference the narrator expresses for animal company over human company. Vedder is not making a sentimental claim. The song is positing that the social structures the band found itself inside (radio, MTV, magazine cover photo shoots, parking-lot fan worship) had begun to feel less honest than the ordinary cruelty of nature. The animal in the song is not a symbol of innocence; it is a symbol of legible motivation. Animals do not lie about why they are doing what they are doing.

The arrangement is the most Mookie Blaylock-era thing on Vs. The verse riff is the kind of mid-tempo grunge bedrock the band could have written in their sleep at this point, but the bridge introduces an unusual harmonic pivot that Eddie has called, in a Pearl Jam Radio session in 2007, the moment where the song stops being angry and starts being scared. McCready's solo is one of his shortest on a Vs. track and is, by his own admission in PJ20, the most rehearsed solo he played on the record because he wanted the discomfort of it to read.

Live, 'Animal' has been a regular but not constant presence in setlists since 1993. It tends to be deployed in the first six songs of a show, where it functions as a high-velocity follow-up to whatever opener the band has chosen. At Pacaembu 2005 it was placed third, completing an opening trifecta of 'Go,' 'Hail, Hail,' 'Animal' that was a Vs.-and-No-Code-heavy salvo. South American audiences, who had been waiting more than a decade for this band to come back, treated the placement as a deliberate confession: Pearl Jam was acknowledging that the songs they had been most anxious about (the songs that came out during the height of their resistance to fame) were the ones the audience most needed to hear played.
corduroy:
'Corduroy' is one of the most played live songs in the Pearl Jam catalog, a Vitalogy (1994) album track that has anchored setlists for thirty years. Stone Gossard wrote the music and Vedder wrote the lyric, and the song's origin story is among the most quoted in Pearl Jam lore: Vedder owned a brown corduroy jacket that he had bought used for around twelve dollars in the early 90s. After Ten broke, a department store began retailing a near-identical replica for several hundred dollars, with the implication that buying the jacket would let the customer dress like Eddie Vedder. The song is the band's response to that transaction.

The lyric is therefore not really about a jacket. It is about the more general phenomenon of the band's identity being dismantled and resold back to the world as merchandise. The narrator describes wanting to be left alone, and the wanting itself is the song's argument. Vedder has discussed this in multiple settings (a 1994 Spin cover story is the most cited; he returns to it briefly in PJ20) and has consistently framed 'Corduroy' as a refusal song rather than a complaint song. Refusal is a posture; complaint is an emotion. The song is the posture.

The music is some of Stone Gossard's most architectural writing. The intro is a sequence of harmonics that has become so iconic that audiences sing the guitar line back to the band before the vocal even arrives. The chord changes in the verse work against the rhythm section in a way that is unusual for grunge-era guitar writing; Stone has cited Pete Townshend as the model for that approach. Mike McCready's solo at the end of the song is one of the longest he plays on Vitalogy, and on the studio recording it overlaps with Vedder's vocal in a way that the band would not normally allow.

The song's commercial-resistance posture has become part of its live identity. 'Corduroy' is almost always placed in the first third of a setlist, where it functions as the first true climax of the show. Audiences sing the wordless intro figure with the band, and Vedder routinely lets the audience carry the chorus's title-line phrase by stepping back from the microphone. By the early 2000s this had become a ritual; by 2005 it was a contract between the band and the audience that any 'Corduroy' performance would include this exchange.

At Pacaembu 2005 'Corduroy' arrived fifth in the order, after 'Green Disease' (a Vitalogy deep cut that the band rarely played live) and immediately before 'Given to Fly.' The position is significant. By placing 'Corduroy' fifth, the band signaled that the show was going to be a Vitalogy-inflected reading of the catalog rather than a Ten-inflected one. South American audiences picked this up: the bootleg recording captures a noticeable rise in crowd volume at the opening harmonic that is louder than the response to the previous four songs.
given to fly:
'Given to Fly' is the third track on Yield (1998), the album where Pearl Jam started writing songs for adults rather than for the wounded twenty-four-year-olds who had bought the first three records. Mike McCready wrote the music; Vedder wrote the lyric. The arrangement is heavily indebted to Led Zeppelin's 'Going to California' from Led Zeppelin IV, and McCready has openly acknowledged this debt in multiple interviews including a Guitar World feature in 1998. He has framed it as homage rather than influence: the goal was to write a song that felt, structurally, like a Zeppelin acoustic ballad with electric eruptions.

The lyric is a parable. Vedder describes a figure who is granted the ability to fly, who returns to the ground to share what he has learned, and who is then attacked and stripped by the people he tries to help. The figure has been variously read as a Christ allegory, a Pearl Jam self-portrait (the band as an artist that gives away gifts and is punished for it), and a more general fable about generosity in a hostile world. Vedder has been deliberately non-specific in interviews when asked which reading is correct. In a 1998 Rolling Stone interview promoting Yield, he said only that 'the song is about love,' and refused to elaborate.

Yield as an album was the band's first real reconciliation with its audience after the No Code retreat. McCready has said in PJ20 that 'Given to Fly' was one of the songs that made him feel, during the recording sessions, that the band might survive its own arguments. The band was famously close to breaking up around this period (Jack Irons would leave during the supporting tour due to anxiety attacks; he was replaced by Matt Cameron, the Soundgarden drummer, who has been the band's drummer ever since), and 'Given to Fly' was, in McCready's framing, a kind of gift the band gave itself.

Live, the song occupies a specific position in setlists. It is almost always placed in the first third of a show, where it serves as the first 'lift' moment, an audience-wide vocal that the band uses to gauge the room's energy before deciding how much risk to take in the rest of the set. Vedder typically lets the crowd carry the wordless third of the song, and on good nights this section can run for two minutes longer than the studio recording. McCready frequently extends the closing solo into Hendrix territory; on bootlegs the song can run six minutes despite a four-minute studio length.

At Pacaembu 2005 'Given to Fly' was placed sixth in the running order, after 'Corduroy.' This sequencing tells a story. The band opened the show with three Vs.-and-No-Code-heavy aggressive songs, then dropped to 'Green Disease' (a curiosity), then climbed through 'Corduroy' (the show's first peak) and used 'Given to Fly' as the song that opened the audience up emotionally for what was coming. South American Tour 2005 setlists used 'Given to Fly' in this position consistently across cities, suggesting that the band had landed on a sequence that worked specifically for the continent's reception of their catalog.
green disease:
'Green Disease' is the fifth track on Riot Act (2002), the album that Pearl Jam wrote in the immediate aftermath of two events that defined its emotional weather: the September 11 attacks and the Roskilde Festival tragedy of June 30, 2000, in which nine fans died during the band's set when a crowd surge crushed audience members against the stage. Riot Act is therefore an album about grief and rage at concentrated power. 'Green Disease' is the rage track. The 'green' in the title is the green of money, and the lyric is one of the most direct anti-greed statements the band has ever issued.

Stone Gossard wrote the music; Vedder wrote the lyric. The track is unusually compact for a Riot Act song: under three minutes, with a chorus structure that is almost punk in its insistence on returning to the same hook. This compression is part of the song's argument. Greed, the song claims, is a simple disease with simple symptoms; the music does not need to be complicated to diagnose it. Vedder has discussed the song in a few settings, most directly during the Riot Act tour interviews of 2003, where he framed it as one of the few songs he wrote that came out fully formed in a single sitting.

The context for the song is the early Bush administration. Riot Act was completed in 2002, in the period when the Iraq War was being publicly justified and the Bush tax cuts of 2001 had just been signed into law. The band would soon become one of the most vocal mainstream rock acts opposing the Bush presidency, and 'Green Disease' is part of that body of work alongside 'Bu$hleaguer' (also on Riot Act) and the Vote for Change tour they would join with R.E.M. and Bruce Springsteen in 2004. The song's specific target is the kind of person the band saw as profiting from the post-9/11 climate without being moved by it.

The song has never been a heavy live presence. Riot Act tracks in general circulated less than tracks from Vs. or Yield, partly because Riot Act itself was the worst-selling Pearl Jam album to that date and partly because the band tends to retire its most politically targeted material after the political moment passes. 'Green Disease' has appeared in fewer than a hundred shows in twenty-three years of touring. Its appearances cluster around the Riot Act tour itself and around the South American Tour 2005, which marked a brief Riot Act revival in the band's setlist construction.

At Pacaembu 2005 'Green Disease' arrived fourth in the order, between 'Animal' and 'Corduroy.' This is one of the more interesting placements on the bootleg. Sandwiching a relatively obscure Riot Act track between two of the band's most reliable Vs.-and-Vitalogy crowd-pleasers is a sequencing choice that signals the band wanted Brazilian audiences to hear it. Vedder did not introduce the song or contextualize the lyric, which was unusual for him during this tour; the song was allowed to speak for itself. The placement is one of the small political gestures of the show.
faithfull:
'Faithfull' is the second track on Yield (1998). The intentional doubled letter in the title (which the band has confirmed across multiple interviews is meant to be read as 'faithfull,' not 'faithful') signals the song's central thematic gesture: the surplus letter is a wound, an excess, a thing that should not be there but is. Stone Gossard wrote the music; Vedder wrote the lyric. The song is a critique of religious certainty and, more broadly, of the social structures that organize themselves around the demand for unquestioning loyalty.

Vedder has described himself in interviews from the 1990s and 2000s as agnostic. He grew up in a Catholic household in San Diego before learning, in his late teens, that the man he had been told was his father was not. That biographical fact, which is the seed of 'Alive,' is also the seed of 'Faithfull.' The lyric is suspicious of any system that asks for trust without offering reciprocal honesty. The narrator is not anti-religion; he is anti-deception. The 'truth' of the song is that the social demand for faith is most loudly issued by the institutions least willing to be examined.

Musically, the song is a Stone Gossard exercise in restraint. The verse is a single chord that does not move for several bars before the bridge introduces a half-step lift that releases the tension. The arrangement features one of Mike McCready's most economical guitar performances on Yield: he plays a single repeated figure under the verse and only solos for eight bars at the song's center. Matt Cameron's drumming, which had only recently joined the band when Yield was recorded, is the song's structural engine. Cameron's tendency to play polyrhythmically over a steady beat gives 'Faithfull' the texture that distinguishes it from the more straightforward arrangements on Vitalogy.

The song was a single from Yield, the third released, and received moderate radio play in 1998 before being eclipsed by the more commercially obvious 'Wishlist.' Live, 'Faithfull' has remained in steady but not heavy rotation. It is the kind of song the band brings out when they want the audience to hear them think, rather than to hear them rock. McCready has said in 2007 Pearl Jam Radio that 'Faithfull' is one of his favorite songs to play live precisely because it does not require him to do very much.

At Pacaembu 2005 'Faithfull' arrived eighth in the running order, after 'Even Flow.' The placement is part of a Yield-heavy second quarter of the show. The South American Tour 2005 setlists tended to gather Yield material around this position, which gave the show a particular emotional shape: the audience would experience the band's hardest rock at the start, then hit an introspective pocket of Yield songs in the second quarter, then return to harder material later. 'Faithfull' is the door into that introspective pocket on the Pacaembu bootleg.
untitled:
'Untitled' is the eleventh track on Yield (1998), a largely instrumental piece that the band has historically performed as the opening half of a medley with 'MFC,' which is the album's first track. The pairing is deliberate: in concert, Pearl Jam frequently uses 'Untitled' as a slow ignition point that resolves into the much faster 'MFC.' The Pacaembu 2005 bootleg captures exactly this transition. The two are listed together on the Mookie Blaylock-style audio recording as a single unit ('Untitled + MFC'), which reflects the live performance practice rather than the album sequencing.

The music is Stone Gossard's. The vocal element of 'Untitled' is wordless, a slow descending melodic figure that Vedder typically improvises upon in concert. The studio version is slightly under three minutes; live versions can run to five or six minutes when the band uses the song as space for the audience to settle. Vedder has called 'Untitled' a 'breath song' in interviews, which captures its function: it is a mid-show exhale that prepares the band and the room for the next surge.

The band has occasionally used 'Untitled' as a vehicle for in-show speeches, dedications, or extended improvisations that would interrupt the flow of any other song. Eddie has used the song's space to address Roskilde mourning, to announce political positions during the 2004 Vote for Change tour, and to introduce guests. The song's structural openness is part of why it survived in the live catalog despite never being a single or a fan favorite in the conventional sense.

At Pacaembu 2005 'Untitled' arrived ninth in the order, immediately after 'Faithfull,' and resolved into 'MFC' as the tenth song of the show. The transition is one of the most fluid moments in the bootleg recording: the band moves from the deliberate stillness of 'Untitled' into the high-velocity opening of 'MFC' without a pause, which is the canonical way to deploy this pairing. South American Tour 2005 audiences had not heard the band live in eleven years, and the 'Untitled + MFC' moment served as a kind of breathing-and-exhale that the band built into every show on the tour.
mfc:
'MFC' is the first track on Yield (1998). The title stands for 'Mini Fast Car,' which Vedder confirmed in a 1998 interview with Spin around the album's release. The song is one of the most immediately propulsive things on Yield: a sub-three-minute road song built on a Stone Gossard riff that the band recorded quickly during the Yield sessions in Seattle in 1997. Yield's first track was originally going to be the slower 'Faithfull,' but the band swapped the running order during sequencing to give the album a faster opening, and that decision shaped how the rest of Yield is heard.

Vedder's lyric is one of his shortest on the album. The narrator is driving away from something, and the song is about the specific kind of clarity that arrives in the first hour of a long drive when the place you have left has begun to recede in the rearview but the place you are going has not yet started to look real. This is a Vedder preoccupation that recurs across the catalog (it is the explicit subject of 'Rearviewmirror' on Vs. and the implicit subject of 'Driftin'' on the Into the Wild soundtrack), and 'MFC' is the most concentrated treatment of it.

The arrangement is unusually drum-forward for a 1990s Pearl Jam track. Matt Cameron's first studio recording with the band was Yield, and 'MFC' showcases the rhythmic vocabulary he brought from Soundgarden: complex hi-hat patterns layered over a straight bass-snare-bass-snare backbeat. McCready's guitar is, by his own description in PJ20, deliberately simple on this track. The complexity is in the rhythm section.

Live, 'MFC' has historically been performed as the second half of an 'Untitled + MFC' medley rather than as a standalone song. This pairing has been a Pearl Jam concert convention since the Yield tour of 1998. The transition out of 'Untitled' into 'MFC' is one of the band's reliable applause moments: when the slow descending figure of 'Untitled' resolves into the opening drum fill of 'MFC,' audiences who recognize the move tend to react before Vedder begins to sing.

At Pacaembu 2005 'MFC' arrived tenth in the running order, immediately after 'Untitled.' The transition is captured on the bootleg. The performance is faster than the studio recording, which is consistent with how the band tends to play the song live on tours where they are still calibrating to a new continent's energy. South American Tour 2005 was the band's first proper return to Brazil since 1995, and the pace at which 'MFC' is played on the Pacaembu recording suggests a band that was not yet ready to relax into the room.
porch:
'Porch' is the eighth track on Ten (1991) and one of the most explicitly political songs on a debut album that has otherwise been read, often unfairly, as introspective rather than political. Stone Gossard wrote the music; Vedder wrote the lyric. The song is, in the most direct terms, about reproductive rights. The narrator is responding to the loss of bodily autonomy, and the question that drives the verses is the question of who controls the decisions a person can make about their own body.

Vedder confirmed this reading directly during the band's Saturday Night Live performance on April 11, 1992. While performing 'Porch,' he wrote 'PRO-CHOICE!!!' in marker on his arm and held it up to the camera. The gesture was unscripted and made on live network television, in the period leading up to Planned Parenthood v. Casey, which was being argued before the Supreme Court that same month. The act became one of the defining moments of the band's early public identity. Vedder has discussed the gesture in PJ20 and in subsequent interviews; he has consistently framed it as the only kind of statement he was willing to make in 1992, and a statement he stands by without revision in any later decade.

The music is one of Stone Gossard's most tightly constructed pieces. The verse is built on a single chord with passing tones; the bridge is a sudden harmonic departure that returns immediately to the verse pattern. Mike McCready's solo at the song's climax is, by length, one of the longer guitar features on Ten, and is the moment in the song where the political argument resolves into pure energy. The song's structural climb from verse to bridge to solo is a textbook example of the kind of release-through-loudness that defined the Seattle sound of 1991.

Live, 'Porch' is one of Pearl Jam's defining performance pieces. It is the song most associated with the early-90s footage of Vedder climbing the venue scaffolding, swinging from rafters, and (on a few documented occasions) crowd-surfing while still singing into a wireless microphone. The song's final-minute jam has historically been the band's vehicle for whatever physical risk Vedder was willing to take that night. By 2005, the band's audience had a reasonable expectation that 'Porch' would mark the show's first physical climax even if Vedder no longer climbed venue infrastructure.

At Pacaembu 2005 'Porch' arrived eleventh in the running order, immediately after 'MFC.' The placement is canonical. The bootleg recording captures Vedder's voice at full force on the closing jam, and the performance runs over six minutes against the studio length of just under three and a half. South American Tour 2005 setlists consistently placed 'Porch' in this 10-12 position, which suggests the band had decided in advance that this would be the show's first physical peak in the continent's venues. The Pacaembu performance fulfills that placement.
i got id:
'I Got Id' (sometimes titled 'I Got Shit' on bootlegs and on the original Merkin Ball EP packaging) is one of two songs Pearl Jam recorded with Neil Young in early 1995, immediately after collaborating with Young on his Mirror Ball album. The song was issued in late 1995 as the lead track on the two-song Merkin Ball EP alongside 'Long Road,' and it is the most important non-album track in the Pearl Jam catalog from the mid-90s, partly because of how the recording session itself shaped the band's identity.

The context is significant. Young had invited Pearl Jam to back him on Mirror Ball after the bands had toured together in 1993 and 1995, and the sessions in Seattle in early 1995 produced more material than Mirror Ball could hold. Stone Gossard chose not to participate in the Pearl Jam-credited tracks ('I Got Id' and 'Long Road') for reasons that have been discussed obliquely in interviews and that were largely related to the band's internal debate about how much of itself to merge with Young's project. The song is therefore one of the few Pearl Jam recordings where the rhythm guitar is played by Mike McCready rather than Stone Gossard, and Young himself plays additional guitar on the track.

Vedder's lyric is one of his bleakest. The narrator is in a state of paralysis, unable to act, unable to feel; the song's emotional logic is exhaustion rather than rage. Vedder has discussed the song's mood in interviews from the period as a reflection of where he was personally during the Vitalogy aftermath, which had been the band's most public crisis to date (the protracted Ticketmaster antitrust case, the band's refusal to make music videos for Vitalogy, the constant press speculation about Vedder's mental state). The song does not name any of this, but it is the record of it.

Musically, 'I Got Id' is one of the most unusual recordings in the Pearl Jam catalog because Young's guitar interacts with McCready's in a way the band would not normally allow on a Pearl Jam album. The song is structured around a slow waltz feel that is closer to Crazy Horse than to anything Pearl Jam had recorded to that point. Jack Irons, who was the band's drummer for the Merkin Ball sessions, plays an unusually loose part that hints at the looser playing he would bring to No Code the following year.

Live, 'I Got Id' has been a rare song. It has appeared in fewer than fifty Pearl Jam shows in three decades. Its inclusion in any setlist is therefore a deliberate gesture by the band rather than a routine choice. At Pacaembu 2005 'I Got Id' arrived twelfth in the running order, between 'Porch' and 'Once.' The placement on the bootleg recording suggests the band wanted to use the slow, heavy feel of the song as a deliberate contrast to the explosive 'Porch' that preceded it. The performance is one of the more notable rarities of the South American Tour 2005 catalog, and Brazilian fan recordings of the show consistently flag the moment as one of the surprises of the night.
once:
'Once' is the second track on Ten (1991) and the second installment in what Vedder later named the 'Mamasan' trilogy (the others being 'Alive' and 'Footsteps'). Where 'Alive' described the narrator's discovery that his stepfather was not his biological parent, 'Once' describes the same narrator becoming a serial killer in response to that knowledge. The trilogy is therefore a complete narrative arc: revelation, transformation, capture. Listening to the three songs in order is the canonical way to understand what Vedder was doing on Ten.

The music began life as an instrumental piece written by Stone Gossard and Jeff Ament that the band, when it was still operating as Mookie Blaylock, had been calling 'Agytian Crave.' That demo had been circulated to Vedder along with the demo that would become 'Alive,' and Vedder wrote both lyrics during the same period in late 1990. The two songs share melodic material in their bridges, which is the structural fingerprint of the trilogy. Anyone who has noticed the melodic echo between the two has noticed Vedder's design.

The lyric is a third-person account of the narrator's transformation. The song does not editorialize. It does not condemn the narrator. It does not redeem him. Vedder's instinct in the early Pearl Jam material was to refuse the moralizing posture that grunge-era lyrics often took toward damaged characters; 'Once' is the clearest demonstration of that refusal in the catalog. The narrator is allowed to be terrible, and the music is allowed to be cathartic, and the listener is left to make sense of what that combination means.

Musically, 'Once' is one of the most aggressive things on Ten. Stone Gossard's verse riff is a series of palm-muted descending intervals; the bridge releases the tension into a soloing section that Mike McCready has cited in PJ20 as one of the moments where he found his own voice as a Pearl Jam guitarist rather than a Hendrix imitator. Dave Krusen's drumming on the original recording (Krusen was the band's first drummer, and Ten was the only album he played on) is some of the most punishing work on the album.

Live, 'Once' has historically been one of the band's primary set-openers, alongside 'Go' and 'Release.' The song's wordless intro that becomes the verse riff is a signature start-of-show moment. By 2005, the band had largely retired 'Once' from opener status and was using it more often as a mid-set energy injection. At Pacaembu 2005 'Once' arrived thirteenth in the running order, after 'I Got Id' and before 'Glorified G.' The placement is the inverse of its typical late-90s usage and is one of the structural surprises of the show. The audience response on the bootleg recording suggests Brazilian fans recognized the song instantly and treated its mid-set arrival as a gift.
glorified g:
'Glorified G' is the fourth track on Vs. (1993) and the second of the album's two anti-firearm songs (the first being 'Go'). Where 'Go' addresses the gun directly, 'Glorified G' addresses the gun's owner. The title is the band's compressed name for the kind of person who collects firearms and treats them as accessories of identity rather than as tools or weapons. Stone Gossard wrote the music; Vedder wrote the lyric.

The song's origin is one of the most quoted Pearl Jam stories from the Vs. period. During the Vs. sessions in early 1993, drummer Dave Abbruzzese mentioned in conversation that he had bought a new gun, his second. Vedder's reaction (and the band's reaction more broadly) became the seed of the lyric. Abbruzzese has confirmed this story in subsequent interviews and has noted with some amusement that he played drums on a song that was written about him. The song is therefore not a generalized political statement; it is a specific document of an internal band argument that was happening while the album was being recorded.

The lyric is sarcastic, which is unusual for Vedder. The narrator addresses the gun-collecting figure with mock approval, listing the satisfactions of ownership as if they were virtues. The structure of the irony depends on the listener understanding that Vedder is not endorsing what he is describing. This kind of distance from a position the song is examining is a technique Vedder rarely used; 'Glorified G' is one of the few clearly satirical lyrics in his catalog.

Musically, the song is a Stone Gossard exercise in tight rhythmic writing. The verse is a single-string riff that punches on every beat; the chorus opens up into wider chords. The arrangement is one of the few on Vs. that does not feature an extended Mike McCready solo, which is consistent with the song's compressed length and direct argument. Abbruzzese's drumming on the recording is, perhaps unintentionally, the song's most expressive element: the rhythmic restraint a drummer is required to demonstrate while playing on a song about himself reads, in the recording, as a kind of accidental self-criticism.

'Glorified G' has been a regular but not heavy live presence. The band tends to bring it out during tours when American gun violence is in the news (the song appeared more frequently during the post-Sandy Hook tours of 2013 and 2014, for example). At Pacaembu 2005 'Glorified G' arrived fourteenth in the running order, after 'Once.' The placement is interesting because South American audiences in 2005 did not have the immediate cultural context that American audiences have for the song: gun ownership in Brazil is a different political question than gun ownership in the United States. The band played the song anyway, which suggests they wanted Brazilian listeners to hear how angry the band had been about American gun culture even ten years earlier. The performance is brisk, tight, and lacks the extended solo work that characterizes some of the show's other Vs. tracks.
modern girl:
'Modern Girl' is a Sleater-Kinney song from The Woods (2005), released in May of that year, and Pearl Jam's performance of it during the South American Tour 2005 was an unusual instance of the band covering an active contemporary by another active contemporary. Vedder has been a public admirer of Carrie Brownstein's work since the late 1990s, and the friendship between Vedder and Brownstein (later confirmed during Brownstein's Portlandia and memoir period) was the source of the cover.

The Pacaembu rendition was performed as part of a 'Better Man' interlude rather than as a standalone song. This is a Vedder convention that has shaped many of the band's most celebrated covers: a song the band has not formally rehearsed gets folded into the architecture of one of their existing songs, often during the bridge or the post-bridge breakdown. 'Better Man' is one of Vedder's preferred vehicles for this kind of insertion because the song's tempo and chord progression accommodate a wide range of melodic guests. The Pacaembu bootleg captures the moment when the 'Better Man' arrangement opens up and Vedder begins singing the 'Modern Girl' melody over the band's continuing accompaniment.

The choice of 'Modern Girl' is meaningful. The song, in Sleater-Kinney's original, is a deceptively gentle indie-folk track that contains some of Brownstein's most direct songwriting about consumer culture and gendered economic life. By inserting the song into 'Better Man,' Vedder performed an act of musical conversation: 'Better Man' is one of the most-covered Pearl Jam songs and one of the band's most explicit lyrics about a woman in a damaged relationship, and 'Modern Girl' is one of Sleater-Kinney's most explicit lyrics about a woman in a damaged relationship with capitalism. The two songs talk to each other.

No full studio version of Pearl Jam's 'Modern Girl' exists. The song lives in the bootleg ecosystem of the South American Tour 2005 and a few subsequent performances. The Pacaembu rendition is the most-circulated version among Brazilian Pearl Jam fans, partly because the show was officially released as a soundboard recording on pearljam.com (the band's bootleg series) and partly because the Pacaembu performance is the cleanest insertion of the cover into 'Better Man' on the tour.

At Pacaembu 2005 the 'Modern Girl' fragment occurred during the 'Better Man' performance that arrived seventeenth in the running order. The Pearl Jam audio recording lists this as 'Better Man (Modern Girl)' in track 14, which is the band's standard way of indicating that one song was folded into another in performance. The moment is brief, unannounced, and dependent on listeners knowing the source. For South American fans who had been waiting eleven years for the band to come back, the cover would have been received as a small gift to the part of the audience that had been following the band's musical preferences in the intervening years.
